subject: survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard

messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard
parts:
Hi Folks -

I'm hoping to implement a weibull survival model for some left-censored current-status data where I have the result of a diagnostic test at age a_i telling me whether an individual was infected before that age, but not when. 

I'm hoping to model the actual time of infection on the interval from [0,a_i) as a latent variable, using a weibull proportional hazards model. I want to obtain this value to use as input to another model predicting whether an individual develops disease over some time period.

The only issue is that there is a single time-varying covariate for a discrete exposure event occurring over a 1-year period that will shift the hazard up by a constant over this period.

What I'm worried about is that this discontinuity will mess up stan's gradient calculations for the latent infection time and result in very slow optimization. I'm attaching images showing an example PDF and CDF for an individual with only background exposure up to age 9 and then intensified exposure from age 9-10.

One thought I had was to break the calculation into two pieces, treating the latent infection time as a mixture with one component representing the pre-exposure infection times and the other other the post-exposure times. This would result in 2 latent variables, one from [0,A-1) and another from [A-1,A), so that each would have a continuous domain. But I was wondering if there was a simpler approach that might require less in the way of coding gymnastics?

Thanks!

-Jon

messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: Re: survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard
parts:
Hi everyone - 

I put the question below out on the list and didn't get much traction, and am coming back hat in hand to see if anyone can verify that my solution makes any sense at all.

What I ended up doing, and which seems to recover the right parameters, was to treat the current-status observation of infection for individuals with a postive test (i.e. a positive test, Y = 1, says you were infected at some time before the time of testing, but not when) as a mixture of two latent infection times, one for the period [a,a-1) where a is the individual's current age, and the other from [a-1, a) in which the hazard of infection is known to increase by a constant, which of course introduces a discontinuity into the PDF that I'm concerned will mess up autodiff in stan if I didn't treat this outcome as a mixture. 

If f(x) is the full pdf over the range from [0,a), including both the background exposure and the observed period of elevated exposure from [a-1,a), what I did was to calculate the probability of an infection before A as, where F is the integral of f over the specified range:

Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = (F(0 < t < a_i-1)*f(t_1) /F(0 < t < a_i-1)) +  (F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)*f(t_12 /F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)),

which simplifies to just:

Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = f(t_1) + f(t_2)

This seems to work but I still somehow don't believe it. So I wanted to check and see if you guys thought this was right.

Sorry for any abuse of notation!

Thanks!

-Jon

messages.author: 22d6bf0e16759db6
messages.subject: Re: survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard
parts:
Hi Jon,

Good to see Stan, uh, spreading among disease ecologists. I'm not sure I follow everything you wrote, but let me give it a try...

Key point: am I correct that, if Y_i = 1, then we know that individual i was infected between 0 and testing time a_i ? (I'll leave off the subscript i's from here on out.)

So you start with a piecewise density function f(t), where t is the infection time you want to infer, 0 < t < a, with pieces f1(t) on [0, a-1) and f2(t) on [a-1,a].

And another part of your model, let's say g(s | t) for some additional parameters/data s, depends on t, in such a way that you can't analytically integrate it out, so you need it to be a latent variable.

You split this into two weighted models, and introduce two mutually exclusive latent infection times t1 and t2, assigned their respective pieces of the probability distribution f1(t1) and f2(t2); properly normalized these would be

f1(t1) = f(t1) / F(0, a-1)
f2(t2) = f(t2) / F(a-1, a)

but for Stan's purposes, provided a is a constant, the normalizations can be left out for a bit of extra speed.

[Side confusion: I don't get your notation Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1). Read literally, that looks to me like, "the probability that t is less than a_i if they tested positive", but I thought testing positive implied t < a_i. Perhaps you meant, Pr(t | Y = 1), where t < a_i — in other words, just the density function f(t)? In which case, well, f(t) = f1(t) + f2(t) by definition, since f1(t) is zero from 0 to a-1 and f2(t) is zero from a-1 to a.]

Seems to me you then just need to carry t1, t2 to define a mixed sub-model g(s | t1, t2), so that

g(s | t1, t2) = F(0, a-1) * g(s | t1) + F(a-1, a) * g(s | t2)

since F(0, a-1) and F(a-1, a) are the prior probabilities for t being in [0, a-1) and [a-1, a], respectively. Does that make sense?

Alternatively, you could replace your discontinuous density function with something that's smoothed out at the boundary, e.g.

f(t) = f1(t) * [1 - h(t)] + f2(t) * h(t)

where h(t) is a smoothed step function (say, a narrow logistic) that rapidly goes from 0 to 1 at (a - 1). And then you have a single well-behaved infection time t.

Ed

messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: Re: survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard
parts:
Hi Ed,

Thanks for putting the question more clearly than I did, and you're totally right about the notation re: Pr(t | Y = 1). That's correct and the old version is, on reflection, sort of nonsensical.

Just to clarify, the sequence of events you suggest, if we're sticking with the discontinuous hazard, is:

1. Sample t_1 and t_2 from their mutually exclusive distributions with Pr(t) = h(t)s(t) where h and s are the hazard and survival functions for f1 and f2, respectively.

2. Sample g(s | t1,t2) as you describe, i.e. g(s | t1, t2) = F(0, a-1) * g(s | t1) + F(a-1, a) * g(s | t2).

Just wanted to make sure that including the prior weights in the second step isn't somehow tantamount to double-counting the latent infection times. Don't think it is, just want to be sure.

I like your suggestion about a smooth step function too! Seems like that might be less trouble than dealing with the multiple latent vars.

Thanks!

-Jon

>> What I ended up doing, and which seems to recover the right parameters, was to treat the current-status observation of infection for individuals with a postive test (i.e. a positive test, Y = 1, says you were infected at some time before the time of testing, but not when) as a mixture of two latent infection times, one for the period [a,a-1) where a is the individual's current age, and the other from [a-1, a) in which the hazard of infection is known to increase by a constant, which of course introduces a discontinuity into the PDF that I'm concerned will mess up autodiff in stan if I didn't treat this outcome as a mixture.
>>
>> If f(x) is the full pdf over the range from [0,a), including both the background exposure and the observed period of elevated exposure from [a-1,a), what I did was to calculate the probability of an infection before A as, where F is the integral of f over the specified range:
>>
>> Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = (F(0 < t < a_i-1)*f(t_1) /F(0 < t < a_i-1)) + (F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)*f(t_12 /F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)),
>>
>> which simplifies to just:
>>
>> Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = f(t_1) + f(t_2)
>>
>> This seems to work but I still somehow don't believe it. So I wanted to check and see if you guys thought this was right.
>>
>> Sorry for any abuse of notation!
>>
>> Thanks!
>>
>> -Jon
>>
>> On Friday, May 15, 2015 at 10:31:25 AM UTC-4, Jon Zelner wrote:
>> Hi Folks -
>>
>> I'm hoping to implement a weibull survival model for some left-censored current-status data where I have the result of a diagnostic test at age a_i telling me whether an individual was infected before that age, but not when.
>>
>> I'm hoping to model the actual time of infection on the interval from [0,a_i) as a latent variable, using a weibull proportional hazards model. I want to obtain this value to use as input to another model predicting whether an individual develops disease over some time period.
>>
>> The only issue is that there is a single time-varying covariate for a discrete exposure event occurring over a 1-year period that will shift the hazard up by a constant over this period.
>>
>> What I'm worried about is that this discontinuity will mess up stan's gradient calculations for the latent infection time and result in very slow optimization. I'm attaching images showing an example PDF and CDF for an individual with only background exposure up to age 9 and then intensified exposure from age 9-10.
>>
>> One thought I had was to break the calculation into two pieces, treating the latent infection time as a mixture with one component representing the pre-exposure infection times and the other other the post-exposure times. This would result in 2 latent variables, one from [0,A-1) and another from [A-1,A), so that each would have a continuous domain. But I was wondering if there was a simpler approach that might require less in the way of coding gymnastics?
>>
>> Thanks!
>>
>> -Jon

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard
parts:
Ha, yes. I should use that line more often.

Jon, sounds like we're on the same page. I'm not sure I was ever clear exactly how you were inferring parameter values using your original formulation, but if it was working, perhaps you had something equivalent and I just didn't understand?

And, yeah, smoothing out the step function seems cleaner—one less latent variable per individual, fewer lines of code to screw up, and conceptually the same basic model. (If it changes any of your conclusions, then there are deeper issues at work...)

Ed

> Hi, I just have a generic comment which is that if you’re worried about Stan getting stuck and not getting to the right answer, you can (and should) simulate fake data from your model and then fit data in Stan and check that the assumed parameter values are recovered (up to margin of error).
> A

>> On May 21, 2015, at 3:31 PM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Ed,
>>
>> Thanks for putting the question more clearly than I did, and you're totally right about the notation re: Pr(t | Y = 1). That's correct and the old version is, on reflection, sort of nonsensical.
>>
>> Just to clarify, the sequence of events you suggest, if we're sticking with the discontinuous hazard, is:
>>
>> 1. Sample t_1 and t_2 from their mutually exclusive distributions with Pr(t) = h(t)s(t) where h and s are the hazard and survival functions for f1 and f2, respectively.
>>
>> 2. Sample g(s | t1,t2) as you describe, i.e. g(s | t1, t2) = F(0, a-1) * g(s | t1) + F(a-1, a) * g(s | t2).
>>
>> Just wanted to make sure that including the prior weights in the second step isn't somehow tantamount to double-counting the latent infection times. Don't think it is, just want to be sure.
>>
>> I like your suggestion about a smooth step function too! Seems like that might be less trouble than dealing with the multiple latent vars.
>>
>> Thanks!
>>
>> -Jon
>>

>> On Thursday, May 21, 2015 at 2:49:55 PM UTC-4, Ed Baskerville wrote:
>> Hi Jon,
>>
>> Good to see Stan, uh, spreading among disease ecologists. I'm not sure I follow everything you wrote, but let me give it a try...
>>
>> Key point: am I correct that, if Y_i = 1, then we know that individual i was infected between 0 and testing time a_i ? (I'll leave off the subscript i's from here on out.)
>>
>> So you start with a piecewise density function f(t), where t is the infection time you want to infer, 0 < t < a, with pieces f1(t) on [0, a-1) and f2(t) on [a-1,a].
>>
>> And another part of your model, let's say g(s | t) for some additional parameters/data s, depends on t, in such a way that you can't analytically integrate it out, so you need it to be a latent variable.
>>
>> You split this into two weighted models, and introduce two mutually exclusive latent infection times t1 and t2, assigned their respective pieces of the probability distribution f1(t1) and f2(t2); properly normalized these would be
>>
>> f1(t1) = f(t1) / F(0, a-1)
>> f2(t2) = f(t2) / F(a-1, a)
>>
>> but for Stan's purposes, provided a is a constant, the normalizations can be left out for a bit of extra speed.
>>
>> [Side confusion: I don't get your notation Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1). Read literally, that looks to me like, "the probability that t is less than a_i if they tested positive", but I thought testing positive implied t < a_i. Perhaps you meant, Pr(t | Y = 1), where t < a_i — in other words, just the density function f(t)? In which case, well, f(t) = f1(t) + f2(t) by definition, since f1(t) is zero from 0 to a-1 and f2(t) is zero from a-1 to a.]
>>
>> Seems to me you then just need to carry t1, t2 to define a mixed sub-model g(s | t1, t2), so that
>>
>> g(s | t1, t2) = F(0, a-1) * g(s | t1) + F(a-1, a) * g(s | t2)
>>
>> since F(0, a-1) and F(a-1, a) are the prior probabilities for t being in [0, a-1) and [a-1, a], respectively. Does that make sense?
>>
>> Alternatively, you could replace your discontinuous density function with something that's smoothed out at the boundary, e.g.
>>
>> f(t) = f1(t) * [1 - h(t)] + f2(t) * h(t)
>>
>> where h(t) is a smoothed step function (say, a narrow logistic) that rapidly goes from 0 to 1 at (a - 1). And then you have a single well-behaved infection time t.
>>
>> Ed
>>
